To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) abstract, “why,” appeals are more persuasive when the decision is temporally remote, and concrete, “how,” appeals are more effective when the decision is proximate, and that (2) these effects seem to be due to a match between the abstractness of a message and the temporal distance of the decision that leads to perceptions that the message feels right.
abstract messages are more persuasive than are concrete messages when the decision is temporally far away, whereas concrete messages are more persuasive when the decision is close.

abstract, “ why -laden appeals are more effective than concrete, “ how -laden appeals when voters’ decision is temporally far away; the reverse is the case when the decision is temporally near, and these effects are stronger for those who are politically naive.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effects of message orientation (abstract vs. concrete) on the persuasiveness of a candidate's political message, and the role played by temporal frame (distant vs. imminent) and message orientation match.
the effects of matching message orientation and temporal frame on the persuasiveness of political messages.
the effects of matching the message orientation with the temporal distance of a political decision on the persuasiveness of a political message.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
abstract, why-oriented appeals are more effective when the decision is temporally distal, and the reverse is true with concrete, how-oriented appeals when the decision is proximal.
a message that matches a voter's temporal distance is more persuasive than one that mismatches.
the effect of matching the message orientation with the temporal frame on political persuasion is that it is more persuasive when voters’ decision is temporally far away than when it is close.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the effect of temporal distance on persuasion is moderated by the abstractness of message content, and that this moderation effect is driven by the match between temporal distance, message abstractness, and fluency.
the abstractness of political messages is more important than the concreteness of the message when the decision is temporally far away.
matching message orientation to temporal distance is critical to political persuasion, and that this effect is driven by a fluency-based heuristic.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of temporal distance on persuasion are not uniform but rather depend on the type of message that is used.
political campaigns need to consider the timing of their message as well as their content to achieve their goals.
candidates who are able to match the abstractness of their message with the temporal distance of the election will be able to persuade more voters.
